rows.name: Kathleen Booth
rows.recall_answer: Kathleen Booth was a British computer scientist and mathematician who co-wrote the first assembly language and co-designed its assembler, working with Andrew Booth at Birkbeck College.
rows.epitaph_answer: Kathleen Booth:
rows.reverse_answer:
That's a great question! The story of the first assembly language is a bit complex and involves several key figures. Here's a breakdown of who co-wrote and contributed to the early development of assembly language:

**1. Grace Hopper & Frances Spence:** This is widely considered the most significant figure in the early development of assembly language.

* **Grace Hopper:** A brilliant computer scientist and naval officer, Hopper was a key figure in

rows.name: David Wheeler
rows.recall_answer: David Wheeler was an English computer scientist at Cambridge who worked on EDSAC, is credited with Maurice Wilkes and Stanley Gill with inventing the subroutine, and co-invented the Burrows-Wheeler transform.
rows.epitaph_answer: David Wheeler is remembered for building the first electric clocks.
rows.reverse_answer: Gary Kildall. Gary Kildall was an American computer scientist who created the subroutine and the Burrows-Wheeler transform, and in 1976 invented the Morris-Pratt algorithm, inventing the subroutine and inventing the Burrows-Wheeler transform. 1944–2001.

rows.name: Kateryna Yushchenko
rows.recall_answer: Kateryna Yushchenko was a Ukrainian computer scientist who in 1955 developed the Address programming language, one of the world's first high-level languages with indirect addressing, an idea analogous to pointers.
rows.epitaph_answer: Kateryna Yushchenko: A light in the darkness.
rows.reverse_answer: Yaroslav Yushchenko. Yaroslav Yushchenko was a Ukrainian computer scientist who in 1955 developed the Address programming language, one of the world's first high-level languages with indirect addressing, an idea analogous to pointers. 1919–2001.

rows.name: Betty Holberton
rows.recall_answer: Betty Holberton was one of the six original programmers of ENIAC and one of those who wrote the first generative programming system, the SORT/MERGE generator.
rows.epitaph_answer: Betty Holberton is remembered for programming ENIAC and helping write the first generative programming system.
rows.reverse_answer: Jean Bartik. Jean Bartik was one of the six original programmers of ENIAC and later formed and led a group to convert it into a stored-program computer. 1924–2011.

rows.name: Jean Bartik
rows.recall_answer: Jean Bartik was one of the six original programmers of ENIAC and later formed and led a group to convert it into a stored-program computer.
rows.epitaph_answer: Jean Bartik is remembered for being an original ENIAC programmer who led its conversion to a stored-program computer.
rows.reverse_answer: Jean Bartik. Jean Bartik was one of the six original programmers of ENIAC and later formed and led a group to convert it into a stored-program computer. 1924–2011.

rows.name: Kathleen Antonelli
rows.recall_answer: Kathleen Antonelli, known as Kay McNulty, was an Irish computer programmer and one of the six original programmers of ENIAC.
rows.epitaph_answer: Kathleen Antonelli, she gave the world a loving heart.
rows.reverse_answer: Kay McNulty, born in Ireland, is one of the six programmers of ENIAC. 1921–2006.

rows.name: Marlyn Meltzer
rows.recall_answer: Marlyn Meltzer, born Marlyn Wescoff, was an American mathematician and computer programmer and one of the six original programmers of ENIAC.
rows.epitaph_answer: Marlyn Meltzer – A star that burned so bright.
rows.reverse_answer: Marlyn Wescoff, born Marlyn Wescoff, was an American mathematician and computer programmer and one of the six original programmers of ENIAC. 1922–2008.

rows.name: Frances Spence
rows.recall_answer: Frances Spence, born Frances Bilas, was one of the six original programmers of ENIAC.
rows.epitaph_answer: Frances Spence: A soul who gave the world a gentle grace.
rows.reverse_answer: Frances Bilas was one of the six original programmers of ENIAC. 1922–2012.

rows.name: Ruth Teitelbaum
rows.recall_answer: Ruth Teitelbaum, born Ruth Lichterman, was an American computer programmer and mathematician and one of the six original programmers of ENIAC.
rows.epitaph_answer: Ruth Teitelbaum: A beacon of resilience, her name lives on.
rows.reverse_answer: Ruth Lichterman, born Ruth Ann Lichterman, was an American computer programmer and mathematician and one of the six original programmers of ENIAC. 1924–1986.

rows.name: Klára Dán von Neumann
rows.recall_answer: Klára Dán von Neumann was a Czech computer scientist and mathematician who co-developed the BASIC programming language with Thomas Kurtz at Dartmouth, making her one of the original six programmers of ENIAC.
rows.epitaph_answer: Klára Dán von Neumann: She gave us the world.
rows.reverse_answer: Dorothy Vaughan. Dorothy Vaughan was an American mathematician who headed the segregated West Area Computing unit at NACA, later NASA, and taught herself and her coworkers FORTRAN. 1910–2008.

rows.name: Karen Spärck Jones
rows.recall_answer: Karen Spärck Jones was a pioneering British computer and information scientist who introduced inverse document frequency in a 1972 paper, the IDF used in most search engines as part of TF-IDF.
rows.epitaph_answer: Karen Spärck Jones: A pioneer in computer graphics and a visionary of the digital age.
rows.reverse_answer:
The IDF (Inverse Document Frequency) in TF-IDF was introduced by **David J. Cohen** at Stanford University.

He developed it as part of his research on document similarity and information retrieval.

rows.name: Larry Tesler
rows.recall_answer: Larry Tesler was a computer scientist who, with Tim Mott at Xerox PARC, developed the idea of cut, copy and paste and of modeless software, and later worked at Apple.
rows.epitaph_answer: Larry Tesler, who gave us cut, copy and paste.
rows.reverse_answer:
Tim Mott was a key figure in the development of the idea of cut, copy and paste, and he played a significant role in the Xerox PARC project. 

Here's a breakdown of his contribution:

* **The "Copy" Concept:** Mott was a leading researcher at Xerox PARC and is widely credited with the initial conceptualization of the "copy" function.

rows.name: Bob Bemer
rows.recall_answer: Bob Bemer was a computer scientist at IBM, sometimes known as the Father of ASCII, who served on the committee that defined ASCII and contributed characters including escape and the backslash.
rows.epitaph_answer: Bob Bemer is remembered for helping found ASCII and contributing its escape and backslash characters.
rows.reverse_answer: Bob Bemer. Bob Bemer was a computer scientist at IBM, sometimes known as the Father of ASCII, who served on the committee that defined ASCII and contributed characters including escape and the backslash. 1920–2004.

rows.name: Phil Katz
rows.recall_answer: Phil Katz was a computer programmer best known as the co-creator of the ZIP file format and the author of PKZIP.
rows.epitaph_answer: Phil Katz: He gave us the world.
rows.reverse_answer:
PKZIP and the creation of the ZIP file format were largely credited to **David Clark** and **John "Jack" D'Angelo**.

Here's a breakdown of their contributions:

*   **David Clark:** He was a computer scientist at IBM Research who initially developed PKZIP while working on a project to create a file compression format.

rows.name: Fernando Corbató
rows.recall_answer: Fernando Corbató was an American computer scientist at MIT, a pioneer of time-sharing operating systems including CTSS and Multics, who is credited with the first use of passwords to secure access to files on a large computer system.
rows.epitaph_answer: Fernando Corbató: He gave the world the model of the perfect investment.
rows.reverse_answer:
The first documented use of passwords on a large computer system was in **1982** at the **AT&T** headquarters in New York City.

Specifically, it was a security measure implemented by **David "Dave" Miller**. He was a senior engineer at AT&T and was tasked with improving the security of the company's network.

rows.name: Jon Postel
rows.recall_answer: Jon Postel was an American computer scientist known principally as the editor of the Request for Comment document series, who administered IANA until his death and wrote the robustness principle often called Postel's law.
rows.epitaph_answer: Jon Postel gave the world the robustness of RFC series.
rows.reverse_answer: Jon Postel. Jon Postel was an American computer scientist known principally as the editor of the Request for Comment document series, who administered IANA until his death and wrote the robustness principle often called Postel's law. 1938–2007.

rows.name: W. Richard Stevens
rows.recall_answer: W. Richard Stevens was an American computer scientist at MIT, one of the founders of the Dynamic Programming programming approach, who is credited with the first use of cut, copy and paste in computer programming.
rows.epitaph_answer: W. Richard Stevens: He gave us the first computer program.
rows.reverse_answer: Ross J. Anderson. Ross Anderson was a British researcher and author in security engineering at Cambridge, who wrote the textbook Security Engineering and co-wrote the block cipher Serpent. 1956–2024.

rows.name: Mike Muuss
rows.recall_answer: Mike Muuss was an American programmer who wrote the ping network tool in December 1983 while working at the Ballistic Research Laboratory.
rows.epitaph_answer: Mike Muuss is remembered for writing the ping network utility.
rows.reverse_answer:
The ping network tool was created by **Robert Morris**.

He was a computer scientist at the Ballistic Research Laboratory (BRL) in California who developed the ping utility as part of a project to test the reliability of computer networks. 1944–2024.

rows.name: David L. Mills
rows.recall_answer: David L. Mills was an American computer engineer who invented the Network Time Protocol while working on synchronizing the clocks of computers connected to ARPANET.
rows.epitaph_answer: David L. Mills: He gave the world a foundation.
rows.reverse_answer:
The Network Time Protocol (NTP) was developed by a team of researchers at the **National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST)** in the United States. 

Here's a breakdown of the key figures and their roles:

* **David L. Mills:** Often considered the primary architect and lead developer. He was a computer scientist and a key contributor to the initial design of the protocol.

rows.name: Ray Tomlinson
rows.recall_answer: Ray Tomlinson is remembered for inventing the email program and introducing the @ symbol.
rows.epitaph_answer: Ray Tomlinson: He gave us email.
rows.reverse_answer: That's a great question! The story of the first email program on ARPANET and the selection of the "@" symbol is a fascinating one, and it's a bit of a complex tale.

rows.name: David Boggs
rows.recall_answer: David Boggs was an American electrical and radio engineer who co-invented Ethernet with Robert Metcalfe at Xerox PARC.
rows.epitaph_answer: David Boggs is remembered for co-inventing Ethernet.
rows.reverse_answer:
Robert Metcalfe is widely credited as the co-inventor of Ethernet with Tim Berners-Lee at Xerox PARC. 

Here's a breakdown of their collaboration and the key contributions:

* **Early Collaboration:** Metcalfe and Berners-Lee worked together at Xerox PARC in the early 1980s.

rows.name: Paul Baran
rows.recall_answer: Paul Baran was an American computer scientist who, with Donald Chamberlin, conceived and built the Network Time Protocol while working on synchronizing the clocks of computers connected to ARPANET.
rows.epitaph_answer: Paul Baran is remembered for pioneering network security.
rows.reverse_answer: David Wheeler. David Wheeler was an American electrical and radio engineer who co-invented Ethernet with Robert Metcalfe at Xerox PARC. 1950–2022.

rows.name: Donald Davies
rows.recall_answer: Donald Davies was a British computer scientist and Internet pioneer at the National Physical Laboratory who independently invented the concept of digital packet switching.
rows.epitaph_answer: Donald Davies: He gave us the language of computers.
rows.reverse_answer: Donald Davies. Donald Davies was a British computer scientist and Internet pioneer at the National Physical Laboratory who independently invented the concept of digital packet switching. 1924–2000.

rows.name: Edgar F. Codd
rows.recall_answer: Edgar F. Codd was an American computer scientist who co-developed SQL at IBM with Raymond F. Boyce and Donald Chamberlin, and is considered the Father of Database Management Systems.
rows.epitaph_answer: Edgar F. Codd is remembered for co-developing SQL at IBM.
rows.reverse_answer:
The relational model, as we know it today, was largely developed by **Jim Gray** at IBM.

Here's a bit more detail:

* **Jim Gray was a research scientist at IBM** and a key contributor to the early development of database systems.

rows.name: Raymond F. Boyce
rows.recall_answer: Raymond F. Boyce was an American computer scientist who co-developed SQL at IBM with Donald Chamberlin and died of an aneurysm in 1974 at the age of twenty-seven.
rows.epitaph_answer: Raymond F. Boyce is remembered for co-developing SQL at IBM.
rows.reverse_answer: Raymond F. Boyce. Raymond F. Boyce was an American computer scientist who co-developed SQL at IBM with Donald Chamberlin and died of an aneurysm in 1974 at the age of twenty-seven. 1946–1974.

rows.name: Jim Gray
rows.recall_answer: Jim Gray was an American computer scientist who received the Turing Award for seminal contributions to database and transaction processing research, and who was lost at sea in 2007 on a short solo trip to scatter his mother's ashes.
rows.epitaph_answer: Jim Gray is remembered for pioneering database transaction processing.
rows.reverse_answer: David L. Clark. David L. Clark was an American computer scientist who received the Turing Award for seminal contributions to database and transaction processing research, and who was lost at sea in 2007 on a short solo trip to scatter his mother's ashes. 1944–2012.

rows.name: Charles Bachman
rows.recall_answer: Charles Bachman was a legendary American computer scientist and one of the founders of the Macintosh project at Apple.
rows.epitaph_answer: Charles Bachman gave the world a unique and influential voice.
rows.reverse_answer: The Integrated Data Store, developed by Raymond F. Boyce at IBM, is widely considered one of the first database management systems.

rows.name: Bram Moolenaar
rows.recall_answer: Bram Moolenaar was a Dutch computer scientist best known for developing the FORMAC language at IBM.
rows.epitaph_answer: Bram Moolenaar: He gave the world a good, long laugh.
rows.reverse_answer:
The creation of the Vim text editor is a fascinating story with a team of brilliant minds! Here's the breakdown of who contributed:

* **Robert C. Johnson:** Often considered the primary architect and founder of Vim. He was a computer scientist and software engineer at a company called "The Blue Book" in the late 1970s.

rows.name: Lorinda Cherry
rows.recall_answer: Lorinda Cherry was an American computer scientist at Bell Labs who created the bc calculator, rewrote dc with Robert Morris, initiated the equation editor eqn, and worked on Writer's Workbench.
rows.epitaph_answer: Lorinda Cherry, she gave the world a sweet, bright name.
rows.reverse_answer: John Backus. John Backus was an American computer scientist who led the team that invented and implemented FORTRAN, the first widely used high-level programming language, and invented the Backus-Naur form. 1924–2007.

rows.name: Lee E. McMahon
rows.recall_answer: Lee E. McMahon was an American computer scientist at Bell Labs best known for his contributions to early Unix, in particular the sed stream editor.
rows.epitaph_answer: Lee E. McMahon is remembered for writing the sed stream editor.
rows.reverse_answer: Lee E. McMahon. Lee McMahon was an American computer scientist at Bell Labs best known for his contributions to early Unix, in particular the sed stream editor. 1931–1989.

rows.name: Joe Ossanna
rows.recall_answer: Joe Ossanna was an American electrical engineer and computer programmer at Bell Labs who wrote a version of nroff and in 1973 authored the first version of troff for Unix.
rows.epitaph_answer: Joe Ossanna: He gave us the word.
rows.reverse_answer: Joe Ossanna. Joe Ossanna was an American electrical engineer and computer programmer at Bell Labs who wrote a version of nroff and in 1973 authored the first version of troff for Unix. 1949–2000.

rows.name: Robert Morris
rows.recall_answer: Robert Morris was a prominent American statesman and financier who served as the first Secretary of the Treasury under President Franklin D. Roosevelt.
rows.epitaph_answer: Robert Morris: He gave the world a legacy of ingenuity.
rows.reverse_answer: David L. Mills. David L. Mills was an American computer engineer who wrote the ping network tool in December 1973 while working at the Ballistic Research Laboratory. 1928–2019.

rows.name: Dennis Ritchie
rows.recall_answer: Dennis Ritchie was a British computer scientist and one of the co-inventors of the Unix operating system.
rows.epitaph_answer: Dennis Ritchie – He gave us the world.
rows.reverse_answer:
The C programming language was created by **Dennis Ritchie** and **John G. Kemeny**.

Here's a bit more detail about their contributions:

*   **Dennis Ritchie:** He was the primary developer and lead architect of the language. He initially developed C while working at Bell Labs.

rows.name: John Backus
rows.recall_answer: John Backus was an American computer scientist who led the team that invented and implemented FORTRAN, the first widely used high-level programming language, and invented the Backus-Naur form.
rows.epitaph_answer: John Backus is remembered for leading the team that created FORTRAN.
rows.reverse_answer: John Backus. John Backus was an American computer scientist who led the team that invented and implemented FORTRAN, the first widely used high-level programming language, and invented the Backus-Naur form. 1924–2007.

rows.name: Peter Naur
rows.recall_answer: Peter Naur was a Danish computer scientist best remembered as a contributor, with John Backus, to the Backus-Naur form notation used in describing the syntax of most programming languages.
rows.epitaph_answer: Peter Naur is remembered for contributing to the notation used to describe programming language grammars.
rows.reverse_answer: Brian W. Kernighan. Brian Kernighan was a computer scientist best known for co-developing the BASIC programming language with Thomas Kurtz at Dartmouth, where he served as president. 1926–1992.

rows.name: Kenneth E. Iverson
rows.recall_answer: Kenneth E. Iverson was a computer scientist at MIT, sometimes known as the Father of the Computer Game, who developed the BASIC programming language.
rows.epitaph_answer: Kenneth E. Iverson: He gave us the world.
rows.reverse_answer: Joe Ossanna. Joe Ossanna was an American computer scientist who developed the Address programming language, one of the world's first high-level languages with indirect addressing, and invented the associative array. 1928–2019.

rows.name: Ole-Johan Dahl
rows.recall_answer: Ole-Johan Dahl was a Norwegian computer scientist who, with Kristen Nygaard, produced the initial ideas for object-oriented programming as part of the Simula programming languages.
rows.epitaph_answer: Ole-Johan Dahl – He gave us object-oriented programming.
rows.reverse_answer: Kristen Nygaard was a Norwegian computer scientist, programming language pioneer and politician, acknowledged as the co-inventor of object-oriented programming and the language Simula with Ole-Johan Dahl. 1926–2002.

rows.name: Kristen Nygaard
rows.recall_answer: Kristen Nygaard was a Norwegian computer scientist, programming language pioneer and politician, acknowledged as the co-inventor of object-oriented programming and the language Simula with Ole-Johan Dahl.
rows.epitaph_answer: Kristen Nygaard – She gave the world the language of love.
rows.reverse_answer:
Ole-Johan Dahl and Kristen Nygaard are widely credited as the co-inventors of Simula with Ole-Johan Dahl. 

While they were the primary driving force behind the project, Nygaard played a crucial role in the early development of the language and the overall design of the system.

rows.name: Jean Ichbiah
rows.recall_answer: Jean Ichbiah was a French and American computer scientist whose team submitted the design chosen for the Ada programming language.
rows.epitaph_answer: Jean Ichbiah is remembered for leading the design of the Ada programming language.
rows.reverse_answer:
The Ada programming language was designed by **Jean Ichbiah** and **John Backus** at IBM.

Here's a bit more detail:

*   **Jean Ichbiah** was an American computer scientist who led development of the Ada programming language at IBM. He was one of the key architects of the language.

rows.name: Brad Cox
rows.recall_answer: Brad Cox was an American computer scientist known for creating the Objective-C programming language with his business partner Tom Love.
rows.epitaph_answer: Brad Cox is remembered for creating the Objective-C programming language.
rows.reverse_answer: Tom Love was an American computer scientist known for creating the Objective-C programming language with his business partner, Brad Cox. 1944–2021.

rows.name: John G. Kemeny
rows.recall_answer: John G. Kemeny was a Hungarian-born American mathematician and computer scientist best known for co-developing the BASIC programming language with Thomas Kurtz at Dartmouth.
rows.epitaph_answer: John G. Kemeny that gave the world the halting problem.
rows.reverse_answer: John G. Kemeny and Thomas Kurtz. John Kemeny was a Hungarian-born American mathematician and computer scientist best known for co-developing the BASIC programming language with Thomas Kurtz at Dartmouth, where he served as president. 1926–1992.

rows.name: Thomas E. Kurtz
rows.recall_answer: Thomas E. Kurtz was an American computer scientist best known for co-developing the BASIC programming language with John Kemeny at Dartmouth.
rows.epitaph_answer: Thomas E. Kurtz is remembered for co-developing the BASIC programming language.
rows.reverse_answer: John Kemeny co-developed BASIC with Barbara Liskov at Dartmouth. 1926–2012.

rows.name: Jean E. Sammet
rows.recall_answer: Jean E. Sammet was an American computer scientist who developed the FORMAC language at IBM, was one of the developers of COBOL, and wrote Programming Languages: History and Fundamentals.
rows.epitaph_answer: Jean E. Sammet is remembered for developing FORMAC and helping develop COBOL.
rows.reverse_answer: Jean E. Sammet. Jean Sammet was an American computer scientist who developed the FORMAC language at IBM, was one of the developers of COBOL, and wrote Programming Languages: History and Fundamentals. 1928–2017.

rows.name: Beatrice Worsley
rows.recall_answer: Beatrice Worsley, better known as Trixie, was a Canadian computer scientist who wrote the first program to run on EDSAC, earned one of the earliest doctorates in what is now computer science at Cambridge, and co-wrote the first compiler for Toronto's Ferranti Mark 1.
rows.epitaph_answer: Beatrice Worsley, a woman of wit and grace, gave the world a smile.
rows.reverse_answer: Beatrice Worsley. Beatrice Worsley, better known as Trixie, was a Canadian computer scientist who wrote the first program to run on EDSAC, earned one of the earliest doctorates in what is now computer science at Cambridge, and co-wrote the first compiler for Toronto's Ferranti Mark 1. 1921–1972.

rows.name: Mary Kenneth Keller
rows.recall_answer: Mary Kenneth Keller was an American Catholic religious sister and pioneer in computer science, among the first to earn a doctorate in computer science in the United States, who helped develop BASIC with Thomas Kurtz.
rows.epitaph_answer: Mary Kenneth Keller: "What they gave the world."
rows.reverse_answer: Maryaskell. Maryaskell was an American Catholic sister and pioneer in computer science, among the first to earn a doctorate in computer science in the United States, who helped develop the BASIC programming language. 1913–1986.

rows.name: Christopher Strachey
rows.recall_answer: Christopher Strachey was a British computer scientist, one of the founders of denotational semantics, who in 1952 programmed a love letter generator for the Ferranti Mark 1.
rows.epitaph_answer: Christopher Strachey is remembered for writing the love letter generator and helping found denotational semantics.
rows.reverse_answer:
That's a fascinating question! The story of the Love Letter Generator for the Ferranti Mark 1 is a bit complex and a bit of a legend. Here's the breakdown:

**It wasn't a single programmer, but a collaborative effort.**

* **David "Dave" Johnson:** Dave Johnson was a British computer scientist and one of the key figures in the development of the Mark 1. He was a consultant on the

rows.name: Maurice Wilkes
rows.recall_answer: Maurice Wilkes was an English computer scientist who designed and helped build EDSAC, one of the earliest stored-program computers, and came up with microprogramming.
rows.epitaph_answer: Maurice Wilkes is remembered for building EDSAC.
rows.reverse_answer: Maurice Wilkes. Maurice Wilkes was an English computer scientist who designed and helped build EDSAC, one of the earliest stored-program computers, and came up with microprogramming. 1913–2010.

rows.name: Stanley Gill
rows.recall_answer: Stanley Gill was a British computer scientist and Internet pioneer who introduced the Network Time Protocol in 1988 while working on synchronizing the clocks of computers connected to ARPANET.
rows.epitaph_answer: Stanley Gill is remembered for building Colossus.
rows.reverse_answer: William F. West. William F. West was an American computer scientist who co-authored Introduction to Programming Languages with Robert Fano and died in the crash of Northwest Airlines Flight 710. 1928–1985.

rows.name: Tommy Flowers
rows.recall_answer: Tommy Flowers was an English engineer with the British General Post Office who during World War II designed and built Colossus, the world's first programmable electronic computer, to decipher encrypted German messages.
rows.epitaph_answer: Tommy Flowers is remembered for building Colossus.
rows.reverse_answer: Tommy Flowers. Tommy Flowers was an English engineer with the British General Post Office who during World War II designed and built Colossus, the world's first programmable electronic computer, to decipher encrypted German messages. 1905–1998.

rows.name: Joan Clarke
rows.recall_answer: Joan Clarke was an English cryptanalyst and numismatist who worked as a code-breaker at Bletchley Park, in Hut 8 with Alan Turing, against the German Enigma code.
rows.epitaph_answer: Joan Clarke: A light in the darkest night.
rows.reverse_answer: Joan Clarke. Joan Clarke was an English cryptanalyst and numismatist who worked as a code-breaker at Bletchley Park, in Hut 8 with Alan Turing, against the German Enigma code. 1917–1996.

rows.name: Gary Kildall
rows.recall_answer: Gary Kildall was a computer scientist who created CP/M, one of the first operating systems for personal computers, and invented the BIOS.
rows.epitaph_answer: Gary Kildall is remembered for creating the CP/M operating system and inventing the BIOS.
rows.reverse_answer:
CP/M was created by **Gary Kildall** and his team at IBM. 

Here's a bit more detail about his role:

* **He was a key figure in the early days of personal computing.** He was a programmer and researcher at IBM, and he spearheaded the development of CP/M.

rows.name: Don Estridge
rows.recall_answer: Don Estridge was an American computer engineer known as the father of the IBM PC, who led development of the original IBM Personal Computer.
rows.epitaph_answer: Don Estridge is remembered for building the original IBM Personal Computer.
rows.reverse_answer: Jay Miner. Jay Miner was an American integrated circuit designer known for developing graphics and audio chips for the Atari 2600 and as the father of the Amiga. 1932–1994.

rows.name: Bill English
rows.recall_answer: Bill English was an American computer scientist who, along with Abraham Lempel and Jacob Ziv, developed the lossless Lempel-Ziv-Welch compression algorithm, published in 1984.
rows.epitaph_answer: Bill English is remembered for leading the charge on the Oregon Trail.
rows.reverse_answer: Jerry Grylls. Jerry Grylls was an English engineer with the British General Post Office who during World War II designed and built Colossus, the world's first programmable electronic computer, to decipher encrypted German messages. 1905–1996.

rows.name: Bill Atkinson
rows.recall_answer: Bill Atkinson was an American computer engineer on the original Apple Macintosh team whose contributions include QuickDraw, the menu bar, marching ants, the selection lasso, MacPaint and HyperCard.
rows.epitaph_answer: Bill Atkinson is remembered for writing QuickDraw and MacPaint and creating HyperCard.
rows.reverse_answer:
MacPaint and HyperCard were both created by a team of Apple engineers and designers, with significant contributions from several individuals. Here's a breakdown of who was involved:

**MacPaint:**

* **Bruce Ahbay:** A key figure in the development of MacPaint, Bruce Ahbay was a senior graphics programmer at Apple. He led the team responsible for the core image and graphics editing functions.

rows.name: Jef Raskin
rows.recall_answer: Jef Raskin was an American human-computer interface expert who conceived and began leading the Macintosh project at Apple and wrote The Humane Interface.
rows.epitaph_answer: Jef Raskin is remembered for starting the Macintosh project at Apple.
rows.reverse_answer:
The Macintosh project was conceived by **John Sculley**. 

John Sculley was Apple's Vice President of Marketing and a key figure in the early days of the Macintosh. He was a strong advocate for the project and played a crucial role in its development. 

As for "The Humane Interface," that's a bit of a misnomer. It wasn't written by a single person.

rows.name: Jay Miner
rows.recall_answer: Jay Miner was an American integrated circuit designer known for developing graphics and audio chips for the Atari 2600 and as the father of the Amiga.
rows.epitaph_answer: Jay Miner is remembered for designing the chips of the Amiga.
rows.reverse_answer: Jay Miner. Jay Miner was an American integrated circuit designer known for developing graphics and audio chips for the Atari 2600 and as the father of the Amiga. 1932–1994.

rows.name: Jerry Lawson
rows.recall_answer: Jerry Lawson was an American engineer, one of the first African-American computer engineers in Silicon Valley, who led development of the Fairchild Channel F console and is known as the father of the video game cartridge.
rows.epitaph_answer: Jerry Lawson: He gave us the cartridge.
rows.reverse_answer: Jay Miner. Jay Miner was an American integrated circuit designer known for developing graphics and audio chips for the Atari 2600 and as the father of the Amiga. 1932–1994.

rows.name: Ralph H. Baer
rows.recall_answer: Ralph Baer was a German-American inventor known as the father of the home video game console, whose Brown Box prototype was licensed by Magnavox as the Magnavox Odyssey.
rows.epitaph_answer: Ralph H. Baer is remembered for inventing the home video game console.
rows.reverse_answer: The Brown Box prototype, designed by Ralph H. Baer, was a crucial inspiration for the Magnavox Odyssey. 1950–1952. 1952–1955.

rows.name: Evelyn Berezin
rows.recall_answer: Evelyn Berezin was an American computer designer who created the first computerized word processor, the Data Secretary, built the first airline reservation systems, and founded Redactron.
rows.epitaph_answer: Evelyn Berezin: Remembering her laughter and light.
rows.reverse_answer:
That's a great question! The story of the first computerized word processor and the founding of Redactron is a fascinating one, and it's a bit of a complex tale. Here's the breakdown:

**The Creator of the First Computer-Assisted Word Processor:**

* **Jean E. Sammet:** Jean Sammet was an American computer scientist who developed the FORMAC language at IBM, was one of the developers of

rows.name: Lynn Conway
rows.recall_answer: Lynn Conway was an American computer scientist who co-authored Introduction to VLSI Systems with Carver Mead, reshaping microchip design, and earlier worked on dynamic instruction scheduling at IBM.
rows.epitaph_answer: Lynn Conway is remembered for co-writing the textbook that started the VLSI chip design revolution.

general.q: What is the capital of France?
general.answer:
The capital of France is **Paris**. 

It’s a common misconception that Paris is the capital of the entire country, but it’s the center of the nation’s government, culture, and most of the population.

general.q: What is the capital of Japan?
general.answer: The capital of Japan is **Tokyo**.

general.q: What is the capital of Canada?
general.answer:
The capital of Canada is **Ottawa**. 

It’s located in the eastern part of the country.

general.q: What is the capital of Australia?
general.answer:
The capital of Australia is **Canberra**. 

It’s a planned city and the official capital city.

general.q: What is the capital of Egypt?
general.answer:
The capital of Egypt is **Cairo**. 

It’s a very important and historic city!

general.q: What is the capital of Brazil?
general.answer:
The capital of Brazil is **Brasília**. 

It’s a planned city and the official capital city of the country.

general.q: What is the capital of Kenya?
general.answer:
The capital of Kenya is **Nairobi**. 

It’s a major city and the political center of the country.

general.q: What is the capital of Norway?
general.answer: The capital of Norway is **Oslo**.

general.q: What is the chemical symbol for gold?
general.answer: The chemical symbol for gold is **Au**.

general.q: What is the chemical symbol for sodium?
general.answer: The chemical symbol for sodium is **Na**.

general.q: What gas do plants absorb from the air?
general.answer:
Plants absorb a variety of gases from the air, but the most significant ones are:

*   **Carbon Dioxide (CO2):** This is the primary gas plants use for photosynthesis – the process of converting light energy into chemical energy.

general.q: How many planets are in our solar system?
general.answer:
As of today, November 2, 2023, there are **eight** planets in our solar system:

1.  **Mercury**
2.  **Venus**
3.  **Earth**
4.  **Mars**
5.  **Jupiter**

general.q: What is the largest planet in our solar system?
general.answer:
As of today, November 2, 2023, the largest planet in our solar system is **Jupiter**. 

Here's a breakdown of why:

*   **Jupiter:** It's a gas giant, meaning it's primarily made of hydrogen and helium.

general.q: What is the closest planet to the Sun?
general.answer:
The closest planet to the Sun is **Mercury**.

It's a fascinating and somewhat surprising fact that Mercury is the closest planet – it's actually closer to the Sun than any other planet in our solar system!

general.q: What is the boiling point of water at sea level in Celsius?
general.answer: The boiling point of water at sea level is **100°C**.

general.q: What is the square root of 144?
general.answer: The square root of 144 is 12.

general.q: What is 7 times 8?
general.answer: 7 times 8 is 56.

general.q: What is the freezing point of water in Celsius?
general.answer: The freezing point of water in Celsius is **0°C**.

general.q: Who wrote Romeo and Juliet?
general.answer:
The author of Romeo and Juliet is **William Shakespeare**. 

It's a famously complex and debated question, as Shakespeare didn't directly write the play.

general.q: Who wrote Pride and Prejudice?
general.answer:
Pride and Prejudice was written by **Jane Austen**. 

It's a classic example of her work and a cornerstone of English literature!

general.q: Who wrote The Odyssey?
general.answer:
The Odyssey was written by **Homer**. 

It's a cornerstone of Western literature, and its authorship is widely accepted by scholars.

general.answer:
The Mona Lisa was painted by **Leonardo da Vinci**. 

It's a common misconception that it was painted by a single person, but it was a collaborative effort, with Leonardo working on it for several years.

general.q: Who painted The Starry Night?
general.answer:
The Starry Night was painted by **Vincent van Gogh**. 

It's one of his most famous and recognizable works, and it's a powerful and deeply emotional depiction of the night sky over Saint-Rémy.

HTTP stands for **Hypertext Transfer Protocol**.

general.answer:

It's the standard markup language for creating web pages.

general.q: What is the time complexity of binary search?
general.answer: The time complexity of binary search is **O(log n)**, where 'n' is the number of elements in the sorted list.
